vignette:
Amira is thirty-four years old, a divorced mother of two who works the early shift at a large strawberry farm in the Central Valley. She has been here for six years, ever since she left her husband and moved her children from the city to a small rented house near the fields. She prefers the quiet of the rural mornings, the rows of green stretching out under the fog. But that quiet has not felt safe for the last eighteen months.

It happened in late April, during the first big harvest. Amira was working the packing line near the conveyor belt that runs from the field into the shed. Her friend Maria, a woman from Oaxaca who always shared her tortillas at lunch, was assigned to the belt that morning. Amira remembers the sound of the motor, the chatter of the other women, the smell of wet earth and diesel. Then a shout, a grinding noise, a scream that did not sound human. Maria’s long sleeve had caught in the roller. Amira saw the arm twist, the bone break through the skin, the blood spray across the white strawberries. She saw Maria’s eyes—wide, unblinking—as the machine pulled her forward. The belt was stopped after maybe five seconds, but those seconds played as hours in Amira’s mind. She still sees Maria’s face every time she closes her eyes.

She did not go back to the farm. Her supervisor called, but Amira said she was sick. Then she said she had found another job. The truth is that she cannot drive past the gravel road that leads to the packing shed without her hands shaking. She now works nights at a small warehouse, stacking boxes of dried fruit. There are no machines, only her hands and a pallet jack. She works alone, and she likes that no one talks to her. The warehouse is silent except for the hum of lights, but Amira still hears the grinding noise when the forklift passes by. She flinches. The other workers have started to notice.

At home, her youngest son, Lalo, asks why she does not cook anymore. She tells him she is tired. She eats standing at the kitchen counter, cold rice from the pot, because the sound of the stove fan reminds her of the belt. She stopped using the blender after she dropped it and shattered the glass, screaming before it even hit the floor. She sleeps on the couch because the bedroom window faces the neighbor’s barn, and the sight of the tractor makes her chest tighten. Her sleep is shallow. She wakes at 3:00 a.m. every night, drenched in sweat, Maria’s scream still fading in the dark. She checks the locks three times, then checks the stove, then checks the locks again. Her ex-husband used to call her paranoid. Now her teenage daughter, Lina, says the same thing.

Amira does not talk about the accident. When her sister calls from Fresno and asks how work is, Amira says fine. She does not tell her about the panic that rises in her throat every time she hears a phone ring—the same ringtone the foreman had when he called to tell Maria’s family. She does not tell her about the guilt that sits in her chest like a stone. She should have pulled Maria away. She should have said something about the loose sleeve. She replays the moment again and again, trying to find a different ending, but there is none.

Yesterday, Lina found her in the backyard, standing by the clothesline, staring at a metal bucket. Amira was not sure how long she had been there. She had seen the bucket and stopped breathing. It was the same color as the hydraulic fluid on the belt. Lina touched her arm and Amira jumped, her heart hammering. “Mom, you scared me,” Lina said. Amira said nothing. She walked inside and sat on the couch, her hands folded in her lap, her eyes fixed on the door. She stayed there until dark.
